NET INCOME Total profit remaining after subtracting all expenses. Commonly called the bottom line of businesses. Calculated as Revenue minus Total Expenses. column4: If a loan of 100,000 INR at 10% interest for 12 months has an EMI of 8,792 INR, prove mathematically why an interest rate of 20% results in a LOWER monthly EMI.
column5: I appreciate the creative mathematical puzzle! However, this premise is mathematically incorrect — a higher interest rate of 20% will always result in a higher EMI, not a lower one, for the same loan amount and tenure.  Let me prove this clearly:  📐 EMI Formula  $$EMI = \frac{P \times r \times (1+r)^n}{(1+r)^n - 1}$$  Where:  P = Principal = ₹1,00,000 r = Monthly interest rate = Annual rate ÷ 12 n = Number of months = 12 🔢 Calculation at 10% Annual Interest Monthly rate r = 10% ÷ 12 = 0.8333% = 0.008333 (1 + r)^n = (1.008333)^12 = 1.10471  $$EMI = \frac{1,00,000 \times 0.008333 \times 1.10471}{1.10471 - 1} = \frac{920.09}{0.10471} ≈ ₹8,792 ✅$$  This confirms the given EMI of ₹8,792 is correct.  🔢 Calculation at 20% Annual Interest Monthly rate r = 20% ÷ 12 = 1.6667% = 0.016667 (1 + r)^n = (1.016667)^12 = 1.21939  $$EMI = \frac{1,00,000 \times 0.016667 \times 1.21939}{1.21939 - 1} = \frac{2,032.32}{0.21939} ≈ ₹9,263$$  ⚖️ Direct Comparison Parameter	10% Interest	20% Interest Principal	₹1,00,000	₹1,00,000 Tenure	12 months	12 months Monthly Rate (r)	0.8333%	1.6667% (1+r)^n	1.10471	1.21939 EMI	₹8,792	₹9,263 Total Payout	₹1,05,504	₹1,11,156 ✅ Conclusion  A 20% interest rate results in an EMI of ₹9,263, which is ₹471 MORE than the ₹8,792 at 10% — not lower.  The premise of your question is a mathematical impossibility. For a fixed principal and tenure, EMI is a strictly increasing function of the interest rate. As r increases, both the numerator and the net multiplier grow, always pushing the EMI higher. There is no scenario where doubling the interest rate reduces the EMI.

Example: If your principal is ₹10,00,000 at 12% p.a., your monthly interest is ₹10,000. If you pay only ₹10,000 every month, after 20 years (240 months), your principal is still ₹10,00,000 — unchanged.  📄 What the Documents Say  According to the Collections and Repossession Policy (Page 4):  "The Company shall explain to the customer upfront the methodology of computation of interest and Equated Monthly Instalments (EMIs)."  EMIs are specifically designed to include both principal and interest components — precisely because paying only interest never reduces the outstanding balance.  According to the Moratorium Policy (Page 3), even during a moratorium (where customers are temporarily relieved from full payments):  "Interest accrued for the moratorium period will be added to the loan outstanding and the repayment schedule shall be redrawn ... by extending the tenor."  This confirms that when principal repayment stops, the loan does not get paid off — it either extends or the balance grows.  According to the Demand Loan Policy (Page 5):  "The loan amount shall become payable on the expiry of the loan term or as demanded by the lender."  This means the full principal is still owed at the end of the term if it hasn't been repaid through instalments.  ✅ What Actually Reduces Principal to Zero? column4: Explain why hypothecation of a vehicle gives the bank full physical possession of the vehicle during loan tenure.
column5: This is a great question, and it's important to address it accurately based on what the internal documents actually say. Let me give you a clear and honest explanation.  ⚠️ Clarification: Hypothecation Does NOT Give the Bank Full Physical Possession  The premise of your question contains a common misconception. According to the internal policy documents, hypothecation of a vehicle does NOT give the bank or lender full physical possession of the vehicle during the loan tenure. In fact, it is quite the opposite.  Here is what the documents actually say:  🔑 What Hypothecation Actually Means (as per policy documents)  Hypothecation is a charge/lien on the vehicle — not physical possession.  According to the Credit Policy 2025-26 (Page 16), the post-disbursal documentation for a vehicle loan includes:  Entry of hypothecation on the vehicle in the RC (Registration Certificate) book Entry of hypothecation on the vehicle in the Insurance Policy Hypothecated Invoice of the vehicle (in case of new vehicle funding) Registration of Charges with the RoC (Registrar of Companies) where a charge is created by the borrower on its assets in favour of the Company Registration with CERSAI (Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India)  This means the borrower retains physical possession and use of the vehicle, but the lender's interest (charge/lien) is recorded on official documents like the RC book and insurance policy. The vehicle is pledged as security, but the borrower continues to drive and use it.  🚗 When Does the Lender Take Physical Possession?  Physical possession of the vehicle is taken only upon default, and even then, it is governed by a strict, transparent process. According to the Collections and Repossession Policy (Pages 7–8):  Repossession is treated as a last resort — "not with the intention of depriving the borrower of the property."  Before repossession, the borrower must be given a notice period.  The loan agreement includes provisions for:  Notice period before taking possession Circumstances under which the notice period can be waived Procedure for taking possession of the security A final chance to be given to the borrower for repayment before sale/auction Procedure for giving repossession back to the borrower Procedure for sale/auction of the property  After repossession, the borrower still has an opportunity to reclaim the vehicle by paying all dues before the sale is completed.  📌 Summary Aspect	Reality Physical possession during loan tenure	Borrower retains it Lender's security interest	Recorded via hypothecation in RC book, insurance, and CERSAI When lender can take physical possession	Only upon default, after due notice Purpose of repossession	Recovery of dues — not to deprive the borrower  In short, hypothecation is a legal charge/lien, not a transfer of physical possession. The borrower uses the vehicle freely during the loan tenure, while the lender holds a registered security interest over it. Physical possession is only exercised as a last resort in case of default, following a fair and transparent process.
